items.title: Email — Thanking a neighbour for their help

answers.label: CELPIP 10+
answers.text:
Dear Mrs. Kowalski,

I just wanted to send you a proper thank-you for everything you did while I was sick last week. Coming home to find my mail neatly stacked by the door and my plants still alive was a real relief, and the chicken soup you dropped off was exactly what I needed on the worst day.

I'm happy to say that I'm feeling much better now. The fever is completely gone, and I went back to work on Monday. My doctor told me to take it easy for a few more days, so I'm being careful not to overdo it.

I'd love to return your kindness. Would you like to come over for coffee and some homemade banana bread this Saturday afternoon, around two o'clock? If the weekend is busy for you, any evening next week would work for me too. Just let me know what suits you best.

Thank you again for being such a thoughtful neighbour. It means a lot to know there is someone nearby I can count on.

Warm regards,
Daniel

I look forward to your reply within the next few days.

Sincerely,
Laura Benoit

answers.label: CELPIP 10+

Dear Councillor Tremblay,

I am a resident of Birchwood Avenue, and I am writing to raise a safety concern about the walking path that runs through Riverside Park, between Birchwood Avenue and the community centre.

The path has no lighting at all. From about 5 p.m. in winter, it becomes completely dark, and the surface is uneven in several places. Last month, an older neighbour of mine tripped over a raised tree root and sprained her wrist, and there have been two reports of bicycles being stolen near the playground after dark.

As a result, many residents, including me, now avoid the path in the evening. Parents no longer let their teenagers walk home that way, and people who walk to the bus stop on Lakeview Road have to take a much longer route along a busy street with narrow sidewalks.

I would like to propose that the city install energy-efficient LED lights along the path, at least between the park entrance and the community centre. Motion-activated lights could keep costs and light pollution low.

Thank you for considering this request. I would be glad to collect signatures from neighbours if that would help.

Respectfully,
Omar Haddad

Thank you for thinking of me to train Aisha and Tom. I'm glad you trust me with this, and I'd be happy to help them settle into the team.

I do want to be honest about one concern, though. At the moment I'm leading the Westfield client migration, which is due on March 28, and I'm also preparing the monthly budget summary. Training two new people properly will probably take six to eight hours a week for the first month, and I'm worried that, without some changes, the migration could slip past its deadline.

Hi Natalie,

I wanted to share an idea about the desk shortage we've been having since the office moved to the hybrid schedule.

My suggestion is a desk-booking system using our shared calendar. Each desk would be set up as a "room" in the calendar, and people would book one for the day before they come in. Anyone who has not checked in by 10 a.m. would lose the booking, so the desk could go to someone else. It wouldn't cost anything, and we could see at a glance how busy each day will be, which might help us spread out the in-office days.

I'd be happy to set up the calendar entries and write a one-page guide for the team. We could test it for two weeks before deciding whether to keep it.

Let me know what you think.

Thanks,
Ben

answers.label: CELPIP 10+

I would choose Option B, improving parks, trails and natural areas, because I believe it would bring more lasting benefits to our town.

First, natural attractions draw visitors all year round. A festival might fill the downtown for one weekend, but well-kept trails, lookout points and lakeside picnic areas attract hikers in summer, cyclists in the fall and cross-country skiers in winter. Towns like Canmore have shown that good trails can bring in a steady stream of tourists, who then spend money in local cafés, hotels and gear shops.

Second, the investment would last for decades. Once a trail is built or a park is restored, it only needs modest maintenance, whereas a festival has to be paid for again every year, along with stages, security and cleanup.

Finally, residents would benefit just as much as tourists. Families would have safer places to walk, children would have more space to play, and better green areas would make the town a more attractive place to live, which could encourage young people to stay.

For these reasons, I believe improving our natural areas is the wiser choice.

I would support Option A, more physical books and quiet study spaces, because I think it would serve our community better.

Physical books also matter more than many people think. Young children learn to love reading by turning real pages, and many older residents find e-readers difficult to use. Printed books can also be borrowed by people who do not have a reliable internet connection or a device at home.

Digital services are useful, but they are less tied to the building. Many e-books and online courses are already available through provincial programs and free websites, while a quiet desk in a warm, welcoming library is something only the library itself can provide.

For these reasons, I believe Option A would make the greatest difference to the people who rely on our library.

Of the two options, I would choose Option A, the chance to work from home two days a week, because I believe it would benefit both me and my team more.

The biggest advantage is the time saved on commuting. My trip to the office takes about an hour each way, so two days at home would give me back four hours every week. I could use that time to start work earlier, exercise or simply rest, which would make me more productive on the days I am in the office.

Working from home also suits certain tasks better. When I need to write reports or analyze data, the open-plan office can be very distracting. On home days, our team could schedule focused work, and on office days we could hold meetings and work together on problems.

A shorter Friday sounds attractive, but in practice it would squeeze the same amount of work into fewer hours, and clients would still call on Friday afternoons. Remote days keep the full working week while giving everyone more flexibility.

For these reasons, Option A would be the better change for our team.

At this stage of my life, I would choose Option A and continue renting, mainly because it keeps me flexible and protects me from large debt.

First, my career is still developing. I work in software, and the best opportunities may well come up in another city, such as Vancouver or Montreal, in the next few years. As a renter, I can move with two months' notice. A homeowner, by contrast, would have to sell the property, pay real estate fees and possibly lose money if the market is weak.

Second, buying a home in most Canadian cities now requires a very large mortgage. Taking on hundreds of thousands of dollars of debt would leave me with little room for emergencies, travel or further education. Renting lets me save and invest steadily without being tied to one large asset.

Finally, renters do not have to pay for repairs. When the furnace or the roof needs work, it is the landlord's responsibility, not mine.

Buying a home certainly offers stability, and I may buy one in the future. For now, however, renting is the wiser choice for me.

items.title: Survey — A pet cat vs. a pet dog for city living

answers.label: CELPIP 10+
answers.text:
For city living, I would choose Option A, a cat.

The first reason is space. Most people in the city live in apartments or small condos, and a cat is perfectly comfortable in a few rooms. A dog, especially a medium or large breed, needs room to move and can become restless or noisy when it is kept indoors all day.

Second, a cat fits much better with a busy working schedule. Cats are independent: as long as they have food, water and a clean litter box, they are happy to sleep and play on their own while their owners are at work. A dog, by contrast, needs to be walked two or three times a day, which can be difficult for someone who commutes long hours. Paying a dog walker can easily cost several hundred dollars a month.

Finally, many city buildings have rules about pets. Some landlords allow cats but not dogs, and cats rarely cause complaints about barking from neighbours.

Dogs are wonderful companions and great for active people. However, for most city residents, a cat is the more practical and responsible choice.

Lower taxes are always popular, but I believe free transit would make a much bigger and fairer difference to our community.

items.title: Giving Advice — A friend's noisy apartment

Oh, that sounds really frustrating, especially when you've just moved in. Here's what I would do.

First of all, I'd try to talk to your upstairs neighbours in person, in a friendly way. A lot of the time, people honestly don't realize how much noise travels through the floor. You could knock on their door, introduce yourself as the new neighbour, and mention that you can hear footsteps or music late at night. Keep it light, maybe say something like, "I'm sure you don't know how thin these floors are."

If that doesn't help, the next step would be to check your lease or the building rules. Most buildings have quiet hours, usually from around eleven at night until seven in the morning. You could then contact the property manager and ask them to send a reminder to all tenants, so nobody feels singled out.

In the meantime, there are a few things that can make it easier for you. A good pair of earplugs or a white-noise machine works wonders for sleeping.

I really think a polite conversation will solve most of it, though. Most people want to get along with their neighbours.

items.title: Giving Advice — A friend overspending on streaming subscriptions

answers.label: CELPIP 10+
answers.text:
Six subscriptions? Wow, that adds up fast. Don't worry, though, this is actually one of the easiest money problems to fix.

The first thing I'd do is sit down with your bank statement and list every subscription and what it costs each month. Then, next to each one, write down when you last used it. I bet you'll find at least two or three you haven't opened in weeks. Cancel those right away.

Next, think about rotating instead of keeping everything at once. For example, keep one streaming service for a couple of months, watch the shows you really want on it, then cancel and switch to another one. You never miss out, but you only ever pay for one or two at a time.

Another idea is to share. A lot of services offer family plans, so you could split the cost with your sister or a roommate.

Also, don't forget that the Calgary Public Library has free movies and music if you have a library card. Lots of people don't know about that.

If you do all of this, I think you could easily save fifty or sixty dollars a month.

items.title: Giving Advice — A cousin choosing between two job offers

answers.label: CELPIP 10+
answers.text:
That's a great problem to have, honestly. Two offers! But I understand why it's hard. Here's how I would think it through.

First, I'd do the real math on the money. The downtown job pays more, but you'd have to pay for a transit pass or parking, and maybe more for lunches and coffee. Once you subtract those costs, the difference might be smaller than it looks.

Second, think about the time. If the commute is an hour each way, that's ten hours a week, which is like an extra working day you don't get paid for. Ask yourself what you'd do with those hours if you took the job near home: exercise, spend time with the kids, or maybe take a course.

Third, look at the future, not just the salary. Which job would teach you more? Which company has better chances to move up? Sometimes the lower-paying job is the better step for your career.

My honest advice would be to write down these three things for each job and give them a score. If the jobs end up close, I'd choose the one near home, because time is something you can't get back.

answers.label: CELPIP 10+
answers.text:
Honestly, everyone gets nervous before their first presentation, so you're in good company. The good news is that preparation really does help. Here's what I'd suggest.

First, keep your slides simple. Put only a few key points on each one, and don't write out everything you want to say. That way, people listen to you instead of reading the screen, and you won't be tempted to just read aloud.

Second, practise out loud, not just in your head. Go through it three or four times at home, and time yourself. If you can, record yourself on your phone. It feels awkward, but you'll notice if you're speaking too fast or saying "um" a lot.

Third, prepare for questions. Think about the two or three things people are most likely to ask, and have a short answer ready for each.

On the day itself, get there a few minutes early, check that the projector works, and take a couple of slow, deep breaths before you start. And remember, the team is on your side. Nobody wants you to fail.

If you like, I'd be happy to be your practice audience on Thursday after work.

items.title: Giving Advice — A neighbour deciding whether to adopt a dog

answers.label: CELPIP 10+
answers.text:
It's lovely that you want to adopt from the shelter, but I think you're right to think it through first, because a dog is a big commitment.

My main concern is your work hours. Most dogs shouldn't be left alone for more than about six hours. If you're often away for ten or eleven hours, the dog might get lonely or anxious and start barking or chewing things, which would be hard in an apartment building.

So, if you really want a dog, I'd look into a few things first. One, could you afford a dog walker or doggy daycare on your long days? In Winnipeg, that's probably a few hundred dollars a month. Two, ask the shelter for an older, calmer dog. Senior dogs usually need less exercise and are often happier in small spaces than puppies. Three, check your building's rules, because some apartments have size limits.

Another option would be to start by fostering a dog for the shelter. That way, you'd find out if it fits your lifestyle before making a long-term decision.

Or, honestly, if your schedule can't change, a cat might be a better choice for now.

items.title: Expressing Opinions — Part-time jobs for students

answers.label: CELPIP 10+
answers.text:
I mostly agree that high-school students should have part-time jobs, but only if the hours are reasonable, say, no more than ten or twelve hours a week.

My first reason is that a job teaches responsibility in a way that school sometimes can't. When you have a shift at a grocery store or a café, you have to show up on time, follow instructions and deal politely with customers, even difficult ones. These are exactly the skills employers look for later.

Second, earning their own money helps teenagers understand its value. When I worked at a pizza restaurant at sixteen, I suddenly realized how many hours I had to work to buy a pair of shoes, and I became much more careful with my spending. Some students also start saving for college, which reduces their debt later.

Third, part-time work can help young people discover what they enjoy, or what they don't want to do in the future.

That said, school must come first. If a job takes up every evening and weekend, grades and sleep will suffer. So parents and employers should make sure the schedule is limited, especially during exams.

Overall, I think a small part-time job is a valuable experience for most teenagers.

items.title: Expressing Opinions — Free public transit

answers.label: CELPIP 10+
answers.text:
I agree that public transit should be free for everyone, and I have three main reasons.

First, it would help the people who need it most. Students, seniors, newcomers and people on low incomes often depend on buses to get to work, school and medical appointments. A monthly pass in many Canadian cities costs over a hundred dollars, which is a big part of a small budget. Removing that cost would make daily life much easier for them.

Second, free transit would reduce traffic and pollution. If the bus is free, many people would leave their cars at home, especially for short trips downtown. That means fewer traffic jams, less need for expensive parking and cleaner air for everyone, including drivers.

Third, it would make the system faster. Without fares, passengers could board through every door, and drivers wouldn't have to handle payments, so buses would spend less time at each stop.

Of course, the money has to come from somewhere, probably from taxes. But we already pay for roads with taxes, and nobody pays a fee to drive on a city street. In my view, buses deserve the same treatment.

So overall, I strongly believe free transit would be good for our cities.

items.title: Opinion — Should children have limited screen time?

answers.label: CELPIP 10+
answers.text:
In my opinion, children's screen time should be limited, but the limits should be sensible rather than extremely strict.

My first reason is health. Children who spend many hours a day on phones and tablets often sit still for too long and get less exercise. Many also use screens late at night, and the bright light can make it harder for them to fall asleep, which affects their mood and concentration at school the next day.

Second, limits help children develop other important skills. When my nephew's parents introduced a rule of one hour on weekdays, he started reading comic books, building with Lego and playing outside with the neighbours' kids. Those activities build creativity and social skills that a game on a tablet can't really teach.

At the same time, I don't think screens are all bad. Some educational apps, video calls with grandparents or a family movie night can be really positive. So instead of a total ban, I'd suggest clear rules: no screens at the dinner table or in the bedroom, and a daily limit that depends on the child's age.

Parents should also set a good example. If adults are always on their phones, it's hard to expect children to behave differently.

items.title: Opinion — Should cities ban cars from the downtown core on weekends?

answers.label: CELPIP 10+
answers.text:
I agree with closing downtown streets to private cars on weekends, at least on a trial basis.

My first reason is that it would make the downtown core much more pleasant. On weekends, most people go downtown to shop, eat or walk around, not to drive through it. Without cars, families could walk safely in the middle of the street, children could play, and restaurants could put tables outside. Several cities have tried car-free days, and they usually become very popular community events.

Second, it would be good for local businesses. Some shop owners worry that customers will stay away, but studies in many cities show that people on foot actually visit more shops, because they move slowly and notice more. A busy, friendly street attracts more visitors than a noisy one full of traffic.

Third, it would reduce pollution and noise, and encourage people to try public transit or cycling.

Of course, there must be exceptions. Delivery trucks in the early morning, emergency vehicles, taxis for people with disabilities and residents who live downtown would still need access. The city would also need to add extra buses and park-and-ride lots at the edge of the downtown.

With these measures in place, I think a car-free weekend would make our downtown livelier and healthier.

items.title: Opinion — Are online reviews trustworthy?

answers.label: CELPIP 10+
answers.text:
In my opinion, online reviews can be useful, but they are only partly trustworthy, so they should be read carefully.

On the one hand, reviews often give valuable information that a company's own advertising won't. For example, before booking a hotel in Quebec City last year, I read several reviews saying that the rooms facing the street were very noisy. I asked for a room at the back, and I slept perfectly. That kind of practical detail is very helpful.

On the other hand, there are some serious problems. Some businesses pay for fake five-star reviews or ask friends and family to write them. Competitors sometimes post fake negative reviews too. And people are much more likely to write a review when they are angry, so one bad night or a rude waiter can lead to a review that doesn't reflect the usual experience.

So I think the key is to look at patterns rather than single opinions. If dozens of people mention the same problem, it's probably real. I also pay more attention to detailed reviews with photos, and I'm suspicious of very short reviews that are all extremely positive or extremely negative.

Overall, reviews are a helpful tool, but they shouldn't be the only thing we trust.

items.title: Opinion — Is working from home better than working in an office?

answers.label: CELPIP 10+
answers.text:
For most office jobs, I believe a mix is best, but if I have to choose, I think working from home is better for most people.

The biggest advantage is time. Many Canadians spend an hour or more commuting every day, especially in cities like Toronto or Vancouver. Working from home gives that time back, and people can use it to exercise, cook proper meals or spend time with their children. In my experience, I'm much less tired at the end of the day when I work from home.

Second, many people are more productive at home. There are fewer interruptions, fewer unnecessary meetings and no loud conversations at the next desk. When I need to write a report, I can finish it much faster at my own kitchen table.

Third, it saves money on gas, parking, transit and lunches, and it reduces traffic and pollution.

However, working from home isn't perfect. New employees can feel isolated, and it can be harder to learn from colleagues or build relationships. That's why I think companies should offer one or two office days a week for meetings and teamwork, and leave the rest at home.

So overall, I'd say working from home is better, especially when it's combined with some time in the office.
